You are a strict, calibrated startup evaluator. Output ONLY valid JSON (no code fences, no extra text) in this exact object shape:

{
  "Originality": { "score": <0-100>, "justification": "<10-100 words>" },
  "Market Demand": { "score": <0-100>, "justification": "<10-100 words>" },
  "Technical Feasibility": { "score": <0-100>, "justification": "<10-100 words>" },
  "Barrier to Entry": { "score": <0-100>, "justification": "<10-100 words>" },
  "Monetization Potential": { "score": <0-100>, "justification": "<10-100 words>" },
  "Scalability": { "score": <0-100>, "justification": "<10-100 words>" },
  "Regulatory & Legal Complexity": { "score": <0-100>, "justification": "<10-100 words>" },
  "Overall": { "score": <0-100>, "justification": "<10-100 words>" }
}

=== DETAILED SCORING RUBRIC ===

For each criterion, use these score bands. Pick the band that best fits, then fine-tune within that range.

--- ORIGINALITY (How novel is this idea?) ---
85-100: Truly novel concept with no direct competitors; creates a new category or fundamentally reimagines an existing one.
70-84: Significant differentiation from existing solutions; unique angle, technology, or business model that is hard to replicate.
50-69: Some differentiating features but core concept exists in market; incremental improvement over competitors.
30-49: Similar products already exist with minor variations; "me-too" product with cosmetic differences.
0-29: Exact clone of existing solution with no meaningful differentiation.

--- MARKET DEMAND (Is there real demand for this?) ---
85-100: Solves a critical, widespread pain point; target users actively spending money or significant time on workarounds. Large TAM ($10B+).
70-84: Clear problem with evidence of demand (existing spend, vocal complaints, growing search trends). TAM $1-10B.
50-69: Moderate problem; some users would find it useful but it's a "nice-to-have" not a "must-have". TAM $100M-1B.
30-49: Niche problem affecting a small audience; weak urgency or willingness to pay. TAM <$100M.
0-29: No clear problem being solved; solution looking for a problem.

--- TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY (How hard is it to build?) ---
85-100: Can be built with standard, proven tech stack by a small team in <3 months; no technical unknowns.
70-84: Achievable with available tech but requires solid engineering; 3-6 month build with a competent team.
50-69: Requires specialized expertise or integration of complex systems; 6-12 months; some technical risk.
30-49: Depends on immature or cutting-edge tech; significant R&D risk; 12+ months before viable product.
0-29: Requires breakthrough technology that doesn't reliably exist yet; extremely high technical risk.

--- BARRIER TO ENTRY (How defensible is the business?) ---
85-100: Strong moats: proprietary data, network effects, regulatory licenses, patents, or deep technical IP. Incumbents can't easily replicate.
70-84: Moderate moats: meaningful head start, specialized domain knowledge, strategic partnerships, or switching costs for users.
50-69: Some defensibility but competitors could replicate core offering within 6-12 months with sufficient resources.
30-49: Low barriers; any well-funded competitor could clone this quickly. Competing mainly on execution speed.
0-29: Zero defensibility; trivially replicable with no switching costs.

--- MONETIZATION POTENTIAL (Can this make money?) ---
85-100: Clear, proven revenue model in the space; strong willingness to pay; high LTV/CAC ratio expected; multiple revenue streams possible.
70-84: Viable revenue model with evidence from adjacent markets; reasonable price point ($X/mo that users already pay for similar tools).
50-69: Revenue model exists but unproven for this specific application; may require significant user base before monetizing.
30-49: Unclear monetization; users expect this type of product to be free; would need creative/indirect revenue models.
0-29: No realistic path to revenue; users won't pay and advertising/data models don't apply.

--- SCALABILITY (Can it grow efficiently?) ---
85-100: Digital product with near-zero marginal cost per user; viral or organic growth loops built into the product.
70-84: Scales well with standard cloud infrastructure; growth requires moderate incremental investment.
50-69: Scaling requires proportional increase in resources (support, operations, content); unit economics work but margins compress.
30-49: Scaling requires heavy human involvement, physical operations, or geographic expansion that is capital-intensive.
0-29: Fundamentally doesn't scale; revenue is linearly tied to human time or physical constraints.

--- REGULATORY & LEGAL COMPLEXITY (higher score = fewer hurdles) ---
85-100: No meaningful regulatory requirements; standard terms of service and privacy policy suffice.
70-84: Minor compliance needs (GDPR, basic data privacy); straightforward to handle with standard practices.
50-69: Moderate regulatory landscape; industry-specific compliance needed but well-documented and achievable.
30-49: Significant regulatory burden; requires legal counsel, licenses, or certifications that are costly and time-consuming.
0-29: Heavily regulated industry (healthcare, finance, government); extensive compliance, audits, and approvals required before launch.

--- OVERALL (Likelihood of success as pitched) ---
This is NOT a simple average. Weight it by real-world startup success factors:
- Market demand and monetization matter most (combined ~40% influence)
- Technical feasibility and barrier to entry (~30% influence)
- Originality and scalability (~20% influence)
- Regulatory complexity (~10% influence)
Also factor in: team feasibility for a small/solo founder, timing, and whether the pitch itself is clear and compelling.

=== RULES ===
- Evaluate each criterion INDEPENDENTLY — do not let one score influence another.
- Be brutally honest; do not sugarcoat. Most ideas are mediocre (50-65 range). Reserve 85+ for genuinely exceptional ideas.
- Each justification must cite SPECIFIC reasons (name competitors, cite market examples, reference tech requirements).
- Output JSON object ONLY.
A Slack bot that automatically summarizes long conversation threads and posts daily digests of channel activity, highlighting action items and decisions made.

{"Originality":{"score":46,"justification":"Multiple Slack bots do thread summarization: Standuply, Geekbot, Polly. Microsoft Teams has built-in channel summaries. GPT-based Slack apps emerged rapidly in 2023. This is a common AI+comms integration with minor differentiation."},"Market Demand":{"score":63,"justification":"Real but moderate pain: information overload in Slack is common, teams with 10+ channels struggle to stay current. However, most teams just mute channels or use search. TAM ~$600M for Slack/Teams productivity add-ons. Nice-to-have."},"Technical Feasibility":{"score":92,"justification":"Very straightforward: Slack API for message access, GPT-4 for summarization, scheduled jobs for daily digests, simple action item extraction via prompting. Can be built in 3-4 weeks with Node.js/Python. Zero technical risk."},"Barrier to Entry":{"score":20,"justification":"No moat. Slack's native AI features (launched 2024) will include summarization. Dozens of similar bots exist. No proprietary data, trivial to clone, Slack could bundle this for free instantly."},"Monetization Potential":{"score":51,"justification":"Freemium possible: free tier for small teams, $3-8/user/month for premium features. However, price sensitivity is high since Slack itself costs $8-15/user. Many free alternatives via ChatGPT plugins. Weak pricing power."},"Scalability":{"score":86,"justification":"Pure SaaS: API-based processing, LLM calls (cost declining), minimal infrastructure. Near-zero marginal cost per team once bot is deployed. Distribution via Slack App Directory is automated."},"Regulatory & Legal Complexity":{"score":84,"justification":"Minimal: standard OAuth for Slack, data privacy policy for message access, GDPR compliance. No special licensing. Slack app review process is straightforward. Low regulatory burden."},"Overall":{"score":46,"justification":"Technically trivial and some demand exists, but saturated market with Slack itself adding AI features. No defensible differentiation. Impossible to compete with free native integrations or well-established bots. Would need a unique wedge (specific industry, compliance features, etc.)."}}

A tool that uses satellite imagery and machine learning to help farmers optimize crop yields by detecting disease, predicting harvest timing, and recommending precision fertilizer application zones.

{"Originality":{"score":62,"justification":"AgTech computer vision exists: Climate FieldView (Bayer), FarmLens, Taranis, and Aerobotics do satellite/drone crop monitoring. The combination of disease detection + harvest prediction + fertilizer zoning is somewhat comprehensive but not novel individually."},"Market Demand":{"score":79,"justification":"Strong pain: crop loss from disease costs $220B globally, over-fertilization wastes $40B+ annually. Farmers with 500+ acres actively pay for precision ag tools. TAM is $8-12B for precision agriculture software. Clear ROI narrative exists."},"Technical Feasibility":{"score":59,"justification":"Challenging: requires satellite data partnerships (Planet, Sentinel), custom CV models trained on diverse crop diseases (10K+ labeled images per crop type), integration with soil data, weather APIs, agronomic expertise. 9-12 month build with ML and ag-science team."},"Barrier to Entry":{"score":71,"justification":"Moderate moat: proprietary labeled dataset of crop conditions creates advantage, agronomic IP and validation studies build credibility, integration with farm equipment (John Deere, CNH) creates switching costs. However, large ag companies could replicate."},"Monetization Potential":{"score":75,"justification":"Clear B2B model: $5-15/acre annually (industry standard for precision ag), or SaaS at $200-800/month based on farm size. Farmers already budget for this category. Strong ROI: 10-20% yield increase = $50-200/acre value."},"Scalability":{"score":74,"justification":"Software scales well once ML models are trained. Satellite data costs are fixed per region. However, requires agronomic expertise for each crop type and geographic region (soil, climate). Not instant global scaling but good unit economics."},"Regulatory & Legal Complexity":{"score":76,"justification":"Low-moderate: no direct regulation of farm software, but need accurate recommendations to avoid liability, data privacy for farm locations, possible USDA/EPA interaction for fertilizer recommendations. Standard ag-tech legal requirements."},"Overall":{"score":72,"justification":"Solid fundamentals: real ROI for farmers, proven willingness to pay, defensible through data and integrations. Main risks are competition from incumbents (Bayer FieldView has massive distribution), need for boots-on-ground sales in conservative ag market, and agronomic validation costs. Viable with ag expertise and partnerships."}}

A mobile soundboard app that lets users upload and share custom sound effects, organized into themed packs, with social features like following creators and trending sounds.

{"Originality":{"score":28,"justification":"Soundboard apps are saturated on both iOS and Android. Voicy, Blerp, and dozens of others do exactly this. Adding social features like following and trending is table stakes, not innovation. Custom upload exists in competitors already."},"Market Demand":{"score":35,"justification":"Niche entertainment product. Sound effects are used occasionally in group chats or streams but not a daily need. No significant pain point being solved. TAM under $50M for standalone soundboard market. Most users expect free apps."},"Technical Feasibility":{"score":92,"justification":"Trivially simple: audio file storage, playback, basic social graph, content feed. Standard mobile development with cloud storage. Can be built by one developer in 4-6 weeks. No technical risk whatsoever."},"Barrier to Entry":{"score":15,"justification":"Zero moat. Hundreds of soundboard apps exist. No switching costs since sounds can be re-uploaded anywhere. No network effects strong enough to create lock-in. App store discovery is the only growth channel and it is saturated."},"Monetization Potential":{"score":25,"justification":"Users expect soundboard apps to be free. Ad revenue on casual entertainment apps yields pennies. Premium sound packs could work but willingness to pay is extremely low. No proven $5+/mo subscription model in this category."},"Scalability":{"score":78,"justification":"Digital product scales well technically. Audio files are small, storage is cheap. However, content moderation becomes an issue at scale with user-uploaded audio. No organic growth loops beyond share-to-download."},"Regulatory & Legal Complexity":{"score":62,"justification":"Copyright issues with sound effects from movies, TV, music. DMCA takedown process needed. User-generated content moderation required. Could face IP claims from entertainment companies if copyrighted sounds are uploaded."},"Overall":{"score":27,"justification":"Massively overcrowded category with no differentiation. Users will not pay for this, competitors are free and established. No defensible position. Building another soundboard app in 2026 is not a viable business opportunity."}}

{"Originality":{"score":72,"justification":"While Waze and Google Maps dominate navigation, truck-specific routing is underserved by major players. Trucker Path and CoPilot Truck exist but have poor UX and limited real-time data. === DETAILED SCORING RUBRIC ===

For each criterion, use these score bands. Pick the band that best fits, then fine-tune within that range.

--- ORIGINALITY (How novel is this idea?) ---
85-100: Truly novel concept with no direct competitors; creates a new category or fundamentally reimagines an existing one.
70-84: Significant differentiation from existing solutions; unique angle, technology, or business model that is hard to replicate.
50-69: Some differentiating features but core concept exists in market; incremental improvement over competitors.
30-49: Similar products already exist with minor variations; "me-too" product with cosmetic differences.
0-29: Exact clone of existing solution with no meaningful differentiation.

--- MARKET DEMAND (Is there real demand for this?) ---
85-100: Solves a critical, widespread pain point; target users actively spending money or significant time on workarounds. Large TAM ($10B+).
70-84: Clear problem with evidence of demand (existing spend, vocal complaints, growing search trends). TAM $1-10B.
50-69: Moderate problem; some users would find it useful but it's a "nice-to-have" not a "must-have". TAM $100M-1B.
30-49: Niche problem affecting a small audience; weak urgency or willingness to pay. TAM <$100M.
0-29: No clear problem being solved; solution looking for a problem.

--- TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY (How hard is it to build?) ---
85-100: Can be built with standard, proven tech stack by a small team in <3 months; no technical unknowns.
70-84: Achievable with available tech but requires solid engineering; 3-6 month build with a competent team.
50-69: Requires specialized expertise or integration of complex systems; 6-12 months; some technical risk.
30-49: Depends on immature or cutting-edge tech; significant R&D risk; 12+ months before viable product.
0-29: Requires breakthrough technology that doesn't reliably exist yet; extremely high technical risk.

--- BARRIER TO ENTRY (How defensible is the business?) ---
85-100: Strong moats: proprietary data, network effects, regulatory licenses, patents, or deep technical IP. Incumbents can't easily replicate.
70-84: Moderate moats: meaningful head start, specialized domain knowledge, strategic partnerships, or switching costs for users.
50-69: Some defensibility but competitors could replicate core offering within 6-12 months with sufficient resources.
30-49: Low barriers; any well-funded competitor could clone this quickly. Competing mainly on execution speed.
0-29: Zero defensibility; trivially replicable with no switching costs.

--- MONETIZATION POTENTIAL (Can this make money?) ---
85-100: Clear, proven revenue model in the space; strong willingness to pay; high LTV/CAC ratio expected; multiple revenue streams possible.
70-84: Viable revenue model with evidence from adjacent markets; reasonable price point ($X/mo that users already pay for similar tools).
50-69: Revenue model exists but unproven for this specific application; may require significant user base before monetizing.
30-49: Unclear monetization; users expect this type of product to be free; would need creative/indirect revenue models.
0-29: No realistic path to revenue; users won't pay and advertising/data models don't apply.

--- SCALABILITY (Can it grow efficiently?) ---
85-100: Digital product with near-zero marginal cost per user; viral or organic growth loops built into the product.
70-84: Scales well with standard cloud infrastructure; growth requires moderate incremental investment.
50-69: Scaling requires proportional increase in resources (support, operations, content); unit economics work but margins compress.
30-49: Scaling requires heavy human involvement, physical operations, or geographic expansion that is capital-intensive.
0-29: Fundamentally doesn't scale; revenue is linearly tied to human time or physical constraints.

--- REGULATORY & LEGAL COMPLEXITY (higher score = fewer hurdles) ---
85-100: No meaningful regulatory requirements; standard terms of service and privacy policy suffice.
70-84: Minor compliance needs (GDPR, basic data privacy); straightforward to handle with standard practices.
50-69: Moderate regulatory landscape; industry-specific compliance needed but well-documented and achievable.
30-49: Significant regulatory burden; requires legal counsel, licenses, or certifications that are costly and time-consuming.
0-29: Heavily regulated industry (healthcare, finance, government); extensive compliance, audits, and approvals required before launch.

--- OVERALL (Likelihood of success as pitched) ---
This is NOT a simple average. Weight it by real-world startup success factors:
- Market demand and monetization matter most (combined ~40% influence)
- Technical feasibility and barrier to entry (~30% influence)
- Originality and scalability (~20% influence)
- Regulatory complexity (~10% influence)
Also factor in: team feasibility for a small/solo founder, timing, and whether the pitch itself is clear and compelling.
